diagram-key.title: The markings you will see
diagram-key.note: This is a key to our diagrams, not a solving proof. Row and column labels give each cell its address.

steps.title: Small digits are candidates
steps.description: R2C4 means row 2, column 4. Candidate 5 sits in the center of its nine small slots. A ring draws your attention to a candidate.

steps.title: Rings identify roles
steps.description: Blue marks the main pattern. Amber separates a second group or role. Neither color means that the candidate is definitely true.

steps.title: Read the result separately
steps.description: A red strike marks a removal. A green ring marks a proved placement. In a hypothetical branch, removals stay conditional until the proof is complete.

candidate-elimination.title: From candidates to a placement
candidate-elimination.note: A schematic part of row 3. These three cells show all their candidates. Other cells are omitted.

steps.title: Two cells reserve two digits
steps.description: R3C4 and R3C5 each contain only 2 and 8. They share a row, so one takes 2 and the other takes 8.

steps.title: Remove both digits from the target
steps.description: The pair uses both digits somewhere in those two cells. Remove 2 and 8 from R3C6, even though the order of the pair is unknown.

steps.title: The remaining candidate is certain
steps.description: Only 5 remains in R3C6. The green ring marks the placement that follows from the red removals.

weak-link.title: Dashed line: at most one is true
weak-link.note: Only the 5s in row 4 are shown. A is R4C2. B is R4C5. A third place remains at R4C8.

steps.title: A and B cannot both be 5
steps.description: The dashed line records a conflict. It does not promise that either endpoint contains 5.

steps.title: If A is true, B is false
steps.description: Suppose R4C2 is 5. The row then rules out every other 5, including B. The arrow shows this direction of reasoning.

steps.title: If A is false, B is still unknown
steps.description: Removing A leaves B and R4C8. Either can still contain 5. A weak link cannot turn a false endpoint into a true endpoint.

strong-link.title: Solid line: at least one is true
strong-link.note: In this separate example, R4C2 and R4C8 are the only places for 5 in the entire row.

steps.title: The row must contain a 5
steps.description: A solid line records a strong link. At least one endpoint must be true. Here the row also prevents both from being true.

steps.title: If A is false, B is true
steps.description: Suppose R4C2 cannot be 5. The solid link forces 5 into R4C8. This is the implication that a strong link supplies.

steps.title: The same pair can supply a weak link
steps.description: If R4C2 is 5, R4C8 cannot be 5. We draw this use as a dashed line. The drawing shows the property used, not a different pair.

wing-cases.title: Two cases, one removal
wing-cases.note: The pivot is R1C1. Wing A is R1C4. Wing B is R4C1. Only these cells and the target show candidates.

steps.title: Start with the pivot {2, 6}
steps.description: The pivot has exactly two choices. The dashed links show the shared candidates that cannot both be true.

steps.title: Case 1: the pivot is 2
steps.description: Wing A loses 2 and must be 9. The target R4C4 sees A through column 4, so it loses 9 in this case.

steps.title: Case 2: the pivot is 6
steps.description: Wing B loses 6 and must be 9. The target sees B through row 4, so it also loses 9 in this case.

steps.title: Keep only the common result
steps.description: Both cases remove 9 from R4C4. That removal is now proved, and the target must be 5. The pivot remains undecided.

uniqueness-swap.title: A swap that preserves every house
uniqueness-swap.note: These four cells are empty in the original puzzle. The large digits show two hypothetical fillings, not givens.

steps.title: First filling
steps.description: Each affected row, column, and box contains one 1 and one 7. The four cells occupy exactly two boxes.

steps.title: Swap every 1 and 7
steps.description: The same houses still contain the same digits. If the first filling completes a classic puzzle, the swapped filling gives a second solution.

chain-walk.title: Read a chain one link at a time
chain-walk.note: Only selected 5s are shown. Rows 1 and 4 each have exactly the two marked places for 5. Other digits are omitted.

steps.title: Match the path to the notation
steps.description: A is R1C1, B is R1C5, C is R4C5, and D is R4C2. Follow A = B - C = D on the board.

steps.title: Assume A is false
steps.description: Temporarily rule out 5 at R1C1. This is an assumption to test, not a removal you can keep yet.

steps.title: Strong: false leads to true
steps.description: Row 1 has only A and B for 5. With A false, B must be true. The solid line matches the equals sign.

steps.title: Weak: true leads to false
steps.description: B and C share column 5. With B true, C must be false. The dashed line matches the minus sign.

steps.title: Strong: false leads to true again
steps.description: Row 4 has only C and D for 5. With C false, D must be true. The chain proves that A false forces D true.

steps.title: Now make a real removal
steps.description: A or D must be true. R2C2 sees A through box 1 and D through column 2. It cannot be 5 in either case.

cell-link.title: A link can stay inside one cell
cell-link.note: R6C4 contains exactly two candidates: 2 and 7. Its small digits are separate statements in a chain.

steps.title: Read (2=7)r6c4
steps.description: The solid line joins two candidates inside R6C4. The equals sign means at least one is true, not that 2 equals 7.

steps.title: Switch digits through the cell
steps.description: If 2 is false, 7 must be true. This lets a chain change digits while staying at the same cell.

steps.title: Use the weak property when needed
steps.description: The cell cannot contain both digits. A dashed link can instead carry the implication from 2 true to 7 false.

als-count.title: Two cells, three distinct digits
als-count.note: R6C4 and R6C5 share a row. All their candidates are shown. Each exclusion below is a separate hypothetical case.

steps.title: One extra digit makes an ALS
steps.description: The cells offer {1, 4, 8}. Two cells need two different digits, so exactly one of those three digits is absent.

steps.title: Suppose the set loses 1
steps.description: R6C4 must be 4. R6C5 then loses 4 and must be 8. The two remaining digits are locked into the set.

steps.title: Suppose the set loses 4
steps.description: Remove every 4 from the set. R6C4 must be 1 and R6C5 must be 8. Losing only one copy of 4 would not be enough.

steps.title: Suppose the set loses 8
steps.description: R6C5 must be 4, which forces R6C4 to be 1. The count alone does not tell us which of these cases is real.

grouped-link.title: Several candidates, one endpoint
grouped-link.note: Only the 5s in row 3 are shown. The two amber rings form G: 5 is in R3C1 or R3C2.

steps.title: Read the whole group
steps.description: The solid link starts between the two amber candidates. It joins the whole statement G to the 5 at R3C8. In (5)r3c12, the group contains 5 in row 3, column 1 or 2.

steps.title: One false member does not make G false
steps.description: Suppose R3C1 loses 5. R3C2 can still satisfy G, so R3C8 is not forced.

steps.title: Every member must be false
steps.description: If both amber candidates lose 5, the group is false. The strong link then forces 5 into R3C8.

rcc-link.title: A weak link between two sets
rcc-link.note: Blue is ALS A: {1, 4, 6} in two cells. Amber is ALS B: {2, 6, 7} in two cells. All their candidates are shown.

steps.title: Every possible 6 in A sees every 6 in B
steps.description: All three 6s share row 8. The dashed line joins the group of blue 6s to the amber 6. Both sets cannot use 6.

steps.title: If B uses 6, A loses every 6
steps.description: Suppose R8C5 is 6. Both blue 6s disappear, leaving 1 and 4 locked in ALS A. The link must reach the whole group.

steps.title: The weak link also allows neither
steps.description: If neither set uses 6, A takes 1 and 4 while B takes 7 and 2. The RCC alone does not force a 6.

steps.title: One unseen occurrence breaks the link
steps.description: Change the example by adding 6 at R9C6. Neither blue 6 sees this new occurrence. The sets still share 6, but it is no longer an RCC.

contradiction.title: A branch must fail for a specific reason
contradiction.note: All candidates of these four cells are shown. Each step after the assumption remains conditional until a contradiction is proved.

steps.title: Start with a statement to test
steps.description: We will test whether R1C1 can be 2. The other three cells each have two candidates.

steps.title: Assume R1C1 is 2
steps.description: R1C4 sees the assumed 2 across row 1. It loses 2 and must be 5.

steps.title: Follow both forced consequences
steps.description: R4C4 loses 5 and becomes 8. R4C1 then loses 8 and becomes 2. Both deductions depend on the original assumption.

steps.title: The contradiction: two 2s in column 1
steps.description: R1C1 and R4C1 cannot both contain 2. The dashed closing link shows the conflict. This branch breaks a Sudoku rule.

steps.title: Discard the assumption and its temporary consequences
steps.description: R1C1 cannot be 2, so it must be 9. Restore the other cells before continuing from the original board.

nested-branches.title: A conclusion stays inside its branch
nested-branches.note: This is a logic map. Each arrow stands for a proved sequence of deductions, not a direct Sudoku link.

steps.title: Both inner cases prove C under A
steps.description: The nested cards keep B and not-B inside the A branch. Their common result proves C only while A is assumed.

children.result: A proved deduction leads to C.
A proved deduction also leads to C.

branches.result: Not checked. C is still unknown in this branch.

steps.title: Every outer case must reach the same result
steps.description: If a separate proof also reaches C when A is false, both outer cases agree. Only then can C be kept on the original board.

children.result: A proved deduction leads to C.
A proved deduction also leads to C.

branches.result: A separate proof reaches C here too.
